sentences.text: This dinosaur possessed a bulky, tank-like body shape completely covered in bony skin ossifications known as osteoderms.
Its skull measured up to half a meter in length, appearing somewhat elongated with a protruding, truncated snout.
Protection for the neck and shoulder area came from three cervical halfrings composed of fused, rounded, rectangular, and asymmetrically keeled bone plates.
When viewed from above, the snout of this animal displays more parallel sides compared to its relative Panoplosaurus.
The creature was a large armored dinosaur reaching approximately 6.6 meters in length and 2 meters in height.
Shoulder spike sizes varied significantly between individuals of E. rugosidens, whereas the spikes on the E. longiceps holotype were relatively small.
Barnum Brown discovered the front half of an armored dinosaur in Alberta, Canada, in 1915.
The genus Edmontonia was first described by Charles H. Sternberg in 1928.
The dinosaur is named after the Edmonton Formation, now known as the Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Canada, where it was first discovered.
The spikes served functions including intimidation, passive protection, and active self-defense against predators.
Researchers suggest the large spikes were used by males to defend territory or gain mates.
Carpenter suggested that larger spikes on specimen AMNH 5665 indicate sexual dimorphism, identifying it as a male.
Carpenter acknowledged that the large spikes might result from ontogeny, where older individuals develop longer spikes.
Traditionally, it was assumed that Edmontonia crouched to protect its vulnerable underbelly from predators.
It is hypothesized that Edmontonia could huddle in groups to minimize attacks on their vulnerable bellies and avoid being flipped by predators.
Studies suggest that Edmontonia and its contemporaries occupied slightly different ecological niches to avoid direct competition for food.
Adult Albertosaurus was the apex predator in the Horseshoe Canyon environment, with juvenile albertosaurs possibly filling intermediate niches.
Petrified wood rings from the time of Edmontonia indicate strong seasonal changes in precipitation and temperature.
Researchers suggest Edmontonia may have died from drought and been rapidly buried by sediment when the rainy season returned.
The type species of the genus Edmontonia is Edmontonia longiceps.
L.S. Russell classified Edmontonia in the family Nodosauridae in 1930, a classification confirmed by later studies.
Robert Thomas Bakker proposed the subgenus Chassternbergia for E. rugosidens in 1988 based on skull proportions and age differences.
Edmontonia lived during the Late Cretaceous Period.
Edmontonia rugosidens lived between 76.5 and 75 million years ago in the lower Dinosaur Park Formation.
Edmontonia rugosidens lived in the Dinosaur Park Formation approximately 76.5 to 75 million years ago.

It is debated whether the shoulder spikes of Edmontonia pointed forward; while Gilmore suggested they shifted during burial, Carpenter and Paul found they could not be rotated without breaking their fit with the rest of the armor.
Carpenter admitted the possibility that the larger spikes were due to ontogeny, as older individuals had longer spikes because the specimen was relatively large.
